newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico's top drug baron confirmed dead.
newsitem.headline: Mexico's top drug baron confirmed dead.

text.p: Amado Carrillo Fuentes, whose death was confirmed by Mexico on Thursday, was a billionaire cocaine king who met an ignominious end in a small hospital.
One of the world's most wanted men, Carrillo dodged police for years, but a decision to undergo plastic surgery to disguise his appearance proved his undoing.
Hours after a long operation at a small Mexico City clinic, a doctor found him dead in bed. The exact cause of his death has still not been determined. Foul play is possible.
Nicknamed "The Lord of the Skies," Carrillo, 42, won fame for his use of passenger jets with stripped-out seats to transport five tons of cocaine at a time undetected from South America to Mexico.

This brazen tactic and the demise of Colombian cartels in past years helped shift the focus in the war on drugs from the jungles of South America to the deserts of northern Mexico on the doorstep of the United States, analysts say.
Thomas Constantine, the head of the U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration, described Carrillo in June 1996 as the most powerful figure in the Mexican drug trade.

Announcing the cocaine king's death last Sunday, Constantine said: "The so-called 'Lord of the Skies' may have escaped earthly justice but I'm sure there is a special place in hell reserved for those like him who have destroyed countless human lives."
Carrillo ran the Juarez Cartel, centred on the northern border city of Ciudad Juarez, across from El Paso, Texas.

Once just in the business of providing "mules" to transport Colombian cartel cocaine, Mexican gangs like the Juarez mob began receiving payment in kind in the 1980s, taking them further into distribution and increasing their clout.

"(The shift) increased their profits by approximately 1,000 percent (and) launched these already formidable crime syndicates on the road to enormous fortunes," Constantine testified before U.S. legislators.

U.S. officials estimated the Juarez Cartel's revenues from drug trafficking at tens of millions of dollars a week -- nearly a third of which was used to bribe government officials on both sides of the border, experts say.

Believed to be a nephew of jailed Guadalajara Cartel drug kingpin Ernesto Fonseca Carrillo, Carrillo seized control of the Juarez gang in April 1993, when its head, Rafael Aguilar Guajardo, was murdered in the tourist resort of Cancun.

Carrillo finally rose to the top of the trafficking heap after the 1996 capture of rival Gulf Cartel kingpin Juan Garcia Abrego, arrested in 1996 and now serving a life sentence without parole in a U.S. prison.
"He moves four times more than other Mexican traffickers," a U.S. official said of Carrillo in 1995. "He handles $60 million in cash the way you or I handle $5."

Although Carrillo maintained a low profile in Mexico, his gang was brutal. On one occasion, U.S. drug agents in El Paso found three bodies in a car trunk with yellow muzzles tied to their mouths in what they took to be a "gift" from the capo.

When Carrillo's pet tiger escaped earlier this year in Ciudad Juarez and police angered the drug capo by handing it over to a zoo, the cartel's victims began turning up tied in yellow ribbons emblazoned with the image of a tiger.

Carrillo began to earn a reputation for narrow escapes. Rival mobsters surprised him as he ate at a Mexico City restaurant in November 1993, but he escaped through a bathroom window amid a hail of bullets.
In January of this year, Carrillo escaped an army raid on his sister's wedding in Sinaloa state, thanks to a tip from an army major who was arrested later.
Carrillo was arrested once -- on Aug. 21, 1989 -- in Guadalajara but was released within weeks, further fanning suspicions that he enjoyed protection in high places.
Also known as the "capo without a face" -- he was rarely photographed -- Carrillo was indicted in Dallas and Miami and had been a fugitive since 1988.
